text: Johnson's praise of Shakespeare rests upon a single principle, which he lays down without ornament: "Nothing can please many, and please long, but just representations of general nature." (Johnson 1765). The writers who shared the stage with Shakespeare drew men, as Johnson describes them, in the shape that the customs of some particular court or city had given them; their figures were cut to the fashion of a season, spoke the cant of a narrow circle, and turned upon the follies of a single year. Such figures could not outlast the occasion that produced them. When the fashion changed they lost their force, and the reader who comes to them afterwards finds little but the dress and furniture of a time that is gone. Shakespeare's persons, in Johnson's view, are made otherwise. They act and speak by those passions and principles which are common to every age and every country; a father's grief or a counsellor's vanity is the same in Elsinore as in London, and the same in one century as in another. Johnson is not blind to the marks which their own day has left upon the plays, and he makes no attempt to deny them. He holds only that these marks lie upon the surface, and that the common nature of mankind lies beneath. For this reason a reader who knows nothing of Elizabethan manners may still believe in Polonius.
